A clean strip of zinc is left standing in blue copper(II) sulfate solution for ten minutes.
(a) Name the type of reaction taking place. [1]
(b) Give two observations. [2]
(c) Write the balanced symbol equation. [3]

steps.working: Zinc is above copper in the reactivity series, so the zinc takes the sulfate and the copper is pushed out. That is a displacement reaction.
steps.decision: Name it before you describe it. Summer 2023 and Summer 2024 both record candidates who described the change perfectly but never wrote the word displacement.

steps.working: First observation: the blue solution fades to colourless.
steps.decision: Copper(II) ions are what make the solution blue; as they leave the solution the blue drains away. Zinc sulfate solution is colourless.

steps.working: Second observation: a brown solid coats the zinc strip.
steps.decision: Name the colour. CCEA has recorded the colour of copper as poorly known in two separate series, and 'a solid forms' on its own is not the mark.

options: Because the mark is for the colour, which identifies the metal
Because a solid always has to be described by its mass
Because copper is the only brown element
whyMenu.explain: An observation has to be specific enough to identify what happened. Brown (or red-brown) says copper.

steps.decision: The sulfate is a spectator, so it travels straight across unchanged. Write all four formulae before balancing.

steps.working: Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu is already balanced: one zinc, one copper, one sulfate on each side.
steps.decision: Check each element before you decide nothing is needed. A one-to-one swap needs no balancing numbers.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) Displacement. (b) The blue solution fades to colourless, and a brown solid forms on the zinc. (c) Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu.

workedExamples.stem:
Iron is extracted from haematite, an ore containing iron(III) oxide, $\ce{Fe2O3}$.
(a) Use the Data Leaflet to calculate the relative formula mass of iron(III) oxide. [2]
(b) In the thermite reaction $\ce{2Al + Fe2O3 -> 2Fe + Al2O3}$, calculate the mass of iron produced from 24.0 g of the oxide. Give your answer to one decimal place. [3]

steps.working: From the Data Leaflet, Fe = 56 and O = 16.
steps.decision: Take both values off the leaflet rather than from memory: the leaflet is the only version CCEA marks against.

steps.working: Fe2O3 has two irons and three oxygens: 2 × 56 + 3 × 16 = 112 + 48 = 160.
steps.decision: Multiply each relative atomic mass by the number of atoms of that element. Missing the 2 in front of the iron is the error Summer 2025's report names.

options: Because the small 2 tells you there are two iron atoms in the formula
Because iron is always counted twice in an oxide
Because the 3 on the oxygen also applies to the iron
whyMenu.explain: A subscript counts the atoms of the element it follows, and nothing else.

steps.working: In the equation, one Fe2O3 gives two Fe, so 160 of oxide gives 2 × 56 = 112 of iron.
steps.decision: Read the ratio off the balanced equation, not off the formula. The 2 in front of Fe is what doubles the iron.
Set it out as one line before you touch the calculator; a written line is what earns the method mark when the arithmetic slips.

steps.working: = 16.8 g, to one decimal place as the question asks.
steps.decision: The accuracy is instructed in the stem, so write it to one decimal place. Summer 2025's report records marks lost for ignoring that instruction.

items.stem: Which metal is higher in the reactivity series, zinc or copper?
items.skill: Prerequisite from the previous topic — you are not expected to have met displacement yet

options.feedback: Zinc is above copper. Everything in this lesson follows from comparisons like that one.
The order runs potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper, so copper is last of the eight. The previous topic builds that list if it is not fixed yet.
No two metals in the series sit at the same height; that is what makes a series useful.

items.stem: In the formula $\ce{CuSO4}$, which part is the sulfate?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.5 — reading a formula that contains a group of atoms

options.feedback: The sulfate is the SO₄ part, and in this lesson it travels from one metal to another without changing.
Cu is copper, the metal. The sulfate is the SO₄ group that follows it.
The sulfur belongs to the group too: sulfate is SO₄ as one unit, not oxygen on its own.

items.stem: When an equation is balanced, what has to be the same on both sides of the arrow?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.5 — what balancing means

options.text: the number of atoms of each element
options.feedback: Atoms are neither made nor destroyed, so each element must be counted equal on both sides.
Two reactants can easily give three products. It is the atoms of each element that must match, not the number of formulae.

options.text: the number of big numbers in front
options.feedback: Those numbers are the tool, not the target. You change them until each element's atom count matches.

items.stem: A strip of zinc is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution and a brown solid forms on it. What type of reaction is this?

options.feedback: Displacement: the more reactive metal has taken the place of the less reactive one.
Neutralisation is an acid and a base making a salt and water. There is no acid here.
Thermal decomposition needs heat to break one compound into two. Here two substances swap partners at room temperature.
Combustion is burning in oxygen. There is no oxygen involved in this tube.

items.stem: Which of these mixtures will not react?

options.text: copper added to zinc sulfate solution
options.feedback: Copper is below zinc, so it cannot push zinc out of its solution. Nothing happens.

options.text: magnesium added to copper(II) sulfate solution
options.feedback: Magnesium is well above copper, so this one does react and copper is displaced.

options.text: zinc added to silver nitrate solution
options.feedback: Zinc is above silver, so the zinc displaces silver from the solution.

options.text: magnesium added to zinc sulfate solution
options.feedback: Magnesium is above zinc, so this reaction happens and zinc is displaced.

items.stem: Zinc is added to silver nitrate solution. What are the products?
items.skill: Write the products of a displacement

options.feedback: The nitrate is a spectator: it stays with whichever metal is in solution, and that is now the zinc.
There is no chlorine anywhere in this mixture. Summer 2024 examiners recorded exactly this answer. The salt keeps its nitrate.
Those are the reactants written out again. Summer 2024's report names that as a common response.
No oxygen is involved. The zinc takes the nitrate and the silver comes out as the metal.

Electrolysis is much more expensive, because of the electrical energy it needs. It is used because carbon will not work.

options.text: aluminium ore does not contain oxygen
options.feedback: Bauxite contains aluminium oxide, so there is oxygen to remove. The question is what can remove it.

options.text: aluminium melts at too low a temperature for a furnace
options.feedback: Melting points are not what decides the method. Reactivity is.

options.text: aluminium is more reactive than iron
options.feedback: That single comparison is the whole answer, and Summer 2023 examiners reported few candidates making it.

options.text: aluminium is a powder, so it has a larger surface area
options.feedback: Surface area changes how fast a reaction goes, not whether it can happen at all.

options.text: iron(III) oxide is unstable at room temperature
options.feedback: Iron(III) oxide is very stable, which is why the mixture needs a fuse to start it.

options.text: aluminium has a lower melting point than iron
options.feedback: True, but not the reason. The reason is that aluminium sits above iron in the reactivity series.

parts.workedSolution: One Fe2O3 gives two Fe, so 160 g of the oxide would give 2 × 56 = 112 g of iron. Scaling down: 24.0 × 112 ÷ 160 = 16.8 g.

parts.stem:
You are given four metals and a solution of a salt of each of them.
Describe how you would use displacement reactions to put the four metals in order of reactivity, and explain how a metal's position in that order decides the way it is extracted from its ore.
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist chemical terms used widely and accurately; organised with clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist chemical vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the intended meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: add a small piece of each metal to each salt solution in a separate test tube
use the same volume and concentration of solution and the same size of metal each time, so it is a fair test
a reaction shows the metal you added is higher in the series than the one already dissolved
the evidence of a reaction is a coating of a new metal, a colour change in the solution or a temperature rise
no change means the added metal is less reactive, so no displacement happens
the metal that displaces all the others is the most reactive and the one that displaces none is the least
a metal above carbon, such as aluminium, must be extracted by electrolysis, because carbon cannot remove its oxygen
a metal below carbon, such as iron, is extracted by heating its ore with carbon, which reduces it

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: The method needs a control as well as a test: say what you keep the same.
Every 'reaction' needs its evidence — what would you actually see?
Finish on carbon: one metal above the line, one below, with a reason for each.
parts.workedSolution: Put a small, clean piece of each metal into a separate test tube holding the same volume of one salt solution, and repeat until every metal has met every solution. Keep the volume and the concentration of the solution and the size of the metal the same each time so that the only thing changed is which metal is used. Watch each tube: a reaction shows that the metal you added is higher in the series than the one already dissolved, and the evidence is a coating of a new metal on the strip, a change in the colour of the solution, or a rise in temperature. A tube in which nothing changes shows that the added metal is less reactive, so no displacement happens. The metal that reacts with every other solution is the most reactive, the metal that reacts with none of them is the least, and the rest fall into place in between. That order also decides how each metal is taken out of its ore. A metal above carbon in the series, such as aluminium, holds its oxygen too tightly for carbon to remove it, so it must be extracted by electrolysis. A metal below carbon, such as iron, can be reduced by heating its ore with carbon, which takes the oxygen away and leaves the metal.

findTheMistake.stem:
Daithí is asked: 'Zinc is added to silver nitrate solution. Complete the word equation and name the type of reaction. [3]'
His answer:
studentWorking: zinc + silver nitrate → zinc chloride + silver
The zinc strip goes grey as silver forms on it, and the solution stays colourless.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: There is no chlorine anywhere in this mixture, so zinc chloride cannot appear. The nitrate is a spectator: it stays in solution and simply changes partners, so the salt formed is zinc nitrate. Summer 2024's examiners recorded 'zinc chloride and silver' as a common response to this very part.
correction: zinc + silver nitrate → zinc nitrate + silver
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the three marks: silver as the second product is right, and so is the name of the reaction. Read the salt you were given and keep its non-metal part — nitrate in, nitrate out.

prompts.prompt: State the rule for displacement reactions of metals in one sentence.
prompts.answer: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt.

prompts.prompt: Give three observations when zinc is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution.
prompts.answer: The blue solution fades to colourless, a brown solid forms on the zinc, and the temperature rises.

prompts.prompt: Complete: zinc + copper(II) sulfate → ______ + ______ , and give the balanced symbol equation.
prompts.answer: Zinc sulfate + copper. In symbols, Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu.

prompts.prompt: Write the balanced symbol equation for the thermite reaction, and say in one clause why it happens.
prompts.answer: 2Al + Fe2O3 → 2Fe + Al2O3, because aluminium is more reactive than iron and so takes the oxygen.

prompts.prompt: What is an ore, and which ore gives iron and which gives aluminium?
prompts.answer: An ore is a rock holding enough of a metal compound to make extracting the metal worthwhile. Haematite gives iron; bauxite gives aluminium.

prompts.prompt: Why is aluminium extracted by electrolysis while iron is extracted with carbon?
prompts.answer: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot take the oxygen from aluminium oxide and electricity has to do it. Iron is less reactive than carbon, so carbon reduces iron(III) oxide to iron.

prompts.prompt: How would you use a grid of metals and salt solutions to rank four metals, and what must you keep the same?
prompts.answer: Add each metal to each salt solution in a separate tube and record whether a reaction happens. A reaction means the added metal is more reactive than the one in solution. Keep the volume and concentration of solution and the size of the metal the same each time.
